analysis.investment_thesis: City Union Bank is exactly the kind of conservative, boring, South Indian regional bank I admire — 120 years old, deeply rooted in its community, and run with capital discipline. However, ROE of only 11.87% and revenue growth of just 6.3% CAGR mean it is not yet compounding at the pace I need to justify accumulation.
key_strengths: Deeply conservative bank with a 120-year track record in Tamil Nadu/South India — the kind of institutional durability that is very hard to replicate
Reasonable valuation at 15.3x trailing P/E and 12.5x forward P/E with P/B of 1.92x — not cheap but not stretched for a quality bank
Total debt has been sharply reduced from INR 5,312 Cr (FY22) to INR 1,790 Cr (FY25), showing disciplined balance sheet management even in a bank context
key_risks: ROE of 11.87% is materially below my 15% threshold — the bank is not generating sufficient returns on shareholders' capital
Revenue CAGR of only 6.3% over 3 years is sub-par; a bank that cannot grow its loan book faster than nominal GDP is losing market share
Finance costs rising at 17.2% CAGR against revenue growing at 6.3% — net interest margin compression risk is real in a rising-rate environment
red_flags: Operating CF was only INR 436 Cr in FY24, down sharply from INR 1,166 Cr in FY22 — earnings quality has been inconsistent
No promoter holding data (typical of old private banks, but absence of a dominant founding owner reduces accountability)
Loan growth modest relative to peers; without accelerating growth, the bank risks being a value trap rather than a compounder
analysis.detailed_analysis:
City Union Bank earns my respect for longevity and conservatism — it has survived many credit cycles by lending carefully in its home market. The valuation is fair, the balance sheet is being cleaned up, and net profit has grown from INR 760 Cr to INR 1,124 Cr over three years, a 13.9% CAGR that is encouraging. However, for a bank to compound wealth, ROE must be consistently above 15%; at 11.87%, too much earnings accretion is absorbed by retained capital rather than returned to shareholders or deployed at high returns.

For long-term holders with patience, CUB at these levels is acceptable — not overpriced, and the franchise is genuine. But I would not add aggressively until I see ROE cross 14-15% and loan growth accelerate. It sits in the 'hold and watch' category for me.
